items.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease has a serum potassium that has risen from 5.0 mmol/L to 6.8 mmol/L (5.0 to 6.8 mEq/L) over 2 days. Which change on the cardiac monitor is typically the EARLIEST ECG sign of this electrolyte imbalance?

options.text: Prominent U waves following flattened T waves
Tall, narrow, peaked T waves
A prolonged QT interval
A sine-wave pattern

rationales.A: Incorrect. Flattened or depressed T waves with prominent U waves are the ECG pattern of hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.
rationales.B: Correct. As potassium rises, tall, symmetric, peaked T waves are usually the first visible ECG change; with further increases the PR interval lengthens, the P wave disappears and the QRS widens.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hyperkalemia tends to shorten, not lengthen, the QT interval. A prolonged QT interval is characteristic of severe hypocalcemia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A sine-wave pattern is a late, pre-arrest finding that appears after QRS widening, just before ventricular fibrillation or asystole; it is not the earliest sign.

items.topic: Hyperkalemia — ECG progression
items.units_note: Potassium in mmol/L is numerically equal to mEq/L.

sources.title: Hyperkalemia
sources.supports: Key B; rationales C (QT shortening) and D (sine wave is the final stage)
sources.evidence: ECG changes often visible when K > 5.5 mmol/L; tall, symmetric, peaked T waves initially; >6.5 mmol/L widened QRS, loss of P wave; finally sine wave then VF/asystole; QT shortening.

sources.title: 10.3 Electrolyte Imbalance (Table 10.7 Hypokalemia and Hyperkalemia)
sources.supports: Key B (tall, peaked T waves in hyperkalemia)
sources.evidence: Hyperkalemia clinical manifestations: tall, peaked T waves, widened QRS complex, prolonged PR interval.

sources.title: Hypokalemia
sources.evidence: Hypokalemia causes ST sagging, T-wave depression and U-wave elevation; T wave shrinks and U wave enlarges as it worsens.

sources.title: Hypocalcemia
sources.evidence: Severe hypocalcemia typically shows prolongation of the QTc and ST intervals.

Note: OpenStax Table 10.7 also lists U waves under hyperkalemia, which conflicts with Merck; that disputed detail is not keyed — U waves are used only as the hypokalemia distractor, supported by Merck.

items.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes who uses insulin reports feeling shaky and sweaty 2 hours before lunch. The client is alert and able to swallow. Capillary blood glucose is 3.1 mmol/L (56 mg/dL). For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated at this time.

rows.text: Give 15 g of carbohydrate as glucose tablets.
Recheck the capillary blood glucose 15 minutes after treatment.
Administer glucagon 1 mg intramuscularly.
Give a second 15 g of carbohydrate immediately, before any recheck, to prevent recurrence.
After the hypoglycemia resolves, offer a snack containing carbohydrate and protein because lunch is more than 1 hour away.

rationales.R1: Indicated. Mild-to-moderate hypoglycemia in a conscious adult is treated with 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate; Diabetes Canada prefers glucose or sucrose tablets or solution.
rationales.R2: Indicated. Blood glucose is retested about 15 minutes after treatment, and another 15 g is given only if it is still low (Diabetes Canada: below 4.0 mmol/L).
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Glucagon 1 mg SC/IM is reserved for severe hypoglycemia when the person cannot take oral carbohydrate (for example, is unconscious) and IV access is not available. This client is alert and can swallow.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Re-treatment depends on the 15-minute recheck. Giving extra carbohydrate without rechecking risks overtreatment, which can cause rebound hyperglycemia and weight gain.
rationales.R5: Indicated. Once hypoglycemia is reversed, a snack with about 15 g of carbohydrate plus a protein source is recommended when the next meal is more than 1 hour away, to prevent recurrence.

items.topic: Hypoglycemia management in a conscious adult (rule of 15)
items.jurisdiction_note: Diabetes Canada defines hypoglycemia (insulin/secretagogue users) as plasma glucose <4.0 mmol/L and re-treats if still <4.0; Merck (US) uses <3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) and re-treats if not >4.4 mmol/L (80 mg/dL). The stem value (3.1 mmol/L) is low under both, and the threshold difference is not tested.
items.units_note: Glucose 3.1 mmol/L × 18 ≈ 56 mg/dL.

sources.title: Hypoglycemia (Clinical Practice Guidelines, Chapter 14)
sources.source_date: 2018 CPG (Can J Diabetes 2018;42 Suppl 1) — no later revision shown on page
sources.evidence: Mild-moderate: 15 g carbohydrate, preferably glucose or sucrose tablets/solution; retest in 15 min, re-treat if <4.0 mmol/L; avoid overtreatment; snack with 15 g carb + protein if meal >1 h away; unconscious without IV: glucagon 1 mg SC/IM.

sources.title: Hypoglycemia
sources.section: Treatment in patients taking antihyperglycemic medications
sources.evidence: Rule of 15s: 15 g glucose or sucrose, recheck at 15 minutes; then a snack with complex carbohydrate and protein; glucagon 1 mg SC/IM (≥25 kg) for those unable to eat or drink.

items.stem: In an Ontario hospital, a 79-year-old client has been found incapable with respect to a proposed surgical treatment. The client's spouse, adult son, and sister are at the bedside. The chart contains a valid power of attorney for personal care that appoints the client's niece and gives her authority over treatment decisions. The niece is capable, available, and willing to act. Under Ontario law, who is the appropriate substitute decision-maker to give or refuse consent for this treatment?

options.text: The client's spouse
The client's niece
The client's adult son
The Public Guardian and Trustee

rationales.A: Incorrect. Under the Health Care Consent Act, 1996, a spouse or partner ranks below an attorney for personal care whose power of attorney covers treatment decisions.
rationales.B: Correct. An attorney for personal care with authority over treatment ranks above a spouse, children and siblings in the Act's list of substitute decision-makers. Because the niece is capable, available and willing, consent is obtained from her as the highest-ranked substitute decision-maker.
rationales.C: Incorrect. A child of the incapable person ranks below both the attorney for personal care and the spouse.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Public Guardian and Trustee decides only as a last resort, when no one on the list meets the requirements to act. A qualified attorney for personal care is available here.

items.topic: Consent — substitute decision-maker hierarchy (HCCA s. 20)
items.jurisdiction_note: Ranking set by Ontario's Health Care Consent Act, 1996, s. 20 (guardian; attorney for personal care; Board-appointed representative; spouse/partner; child or parent; parent with access only; sibling; other relative; PGT as last resort). Other provinces and US states use different surrogate laws; NCLEX items generally use generic advance-directive/health care proxy wording.

sources.title: Health Care Consent Act, 1996, S.O. 1996, c. 2, Sched. A
sources.section: s. 20(1) list of persons who may give or refuse consent; s. 20(2) requirements; s. 20(5) Public Guardian and Trustee

sources.supports: Key B; rationales A, C, D
sources.evidence: s.20(1): 1 guardian; 2 attorney for personal care; 3 Board-appointed representative; 4 spouse/partner; 5 child or parent; 7 brother/sister. s.20(5): PGT decides if no listed person meets s.20(2).

sources.title: Consent (Practice Guideline)

sources.supports: Key B (highest-ranked available, willing SDM); rationale D (PGT last resort)
sources.evidence: If incapable, consent is obtained from the highest ranked available substitute decision-maker from the HCCA hierarchy who is willing; the PGT is the substitute decision-maker of last resort.

items.stem: A client admitted to a medical unit has had a productive cough for 3 weeks with night sweats and weight loss, and active pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected. Which measures should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the client in an airborne infection isolation room with negative air flow.
Wear a fit-tested, seal-checked N95 respirator when entering the room.
Keep the room door closed whether or not the client is in the room.
Have the client wear a mask if transport out of the room is necessary.
Wear a surgical mask instead of a respirator, because tuberculosis spreads by large droplets.
Allow staff who report a previous tuberculosis infection to enter without a respirator.

rationales.A: Correct. Suspected or confirmed pulmonary or laryngeal TB requires Airborne Precautions in a single airborne infection isolation room with negative air flow.
rationales.B: Correct. Staff entering the room of a client with suspected active pulmonary TB must wear a fit-tested, seal-checked N95 (or higher) respirator.
rationales.C: Correct. The door of an airborne isolation room must stay closed to keep the negative-pressure air flow working; Ontario's PIDAC guidance says it is kept closed whether or not the client is in the room.
rationales.D: Correct. Transport out of the room is limited to what is necessary, and the client wears a mask during transport (if tolerated) for source control.
rationales.E: Incorrect. TB spreads by the airborne route in small droplet nuclei that stay suspended in air. A surgical mask does not reliably protect the wearer from inhaling them; an N95 respirator is the minimum.
rationales.F: Incorrect. The N95 requirement for active pulmonary TB applies to all staff. Immunity-based exceptions in Ontario's precautions apply to diseases such as measles and varicella, not TB.

items.jurisdiction_note: Keyed measures agree between Ontario PIDAC and US CDC. One known difference is NOT tested: PIDAC also requires transport staff to wear an N95 for active TB, whereas CDC says transport staff need no mask/respirator if the client is masked.

items.stem: A client with heart failure and peripheral edema has an order for furosemide 40 mg IV now. The vial is labelled furosemide injection 10 mg/mL. How many millilitres should the nurse prepare? Round to the nearest whole number.

rationales.calculation: Volume = dose ordered ÷ concentration = 40 mg ÷ 10 mg/mL = 4 mL. Check: 4 mL × 10 mg/mL = 40 mg. The dose is within the usual initial adult IV dose for edema in the Canadian product monograph and US labelling (20 to 40 mg as a single dose), and IV furosemide is given slowly over 1 to 2 minutes.

items.stem: After removing gloves following a routine bed bath, a nurse's hands are not visibly soiled. According to Ontario PIDAC hand-hygiene guidance (concordant with CDC clinical safety guidance), which action is preferred?

options.text: Wash with soap and running water for at least 2 minutes.
Apply a 70–90% alcohol-based hand rub and rub until dry.
Rinse briefly with water only; no product is needed after glove removal.
Apply a non-alcohol waterless antiseptic foam as first choice.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Soap and water is required when hands are visibly soiled (or in certain spore-related situations). When hands are not visibly soiled, alcohol-based hand rub is preferred.
rationales.B: Correct. When hands are not visibly soiled, a 70–90% alcohol-based hand rub is the preferred method in Ontario health-care settings and is also preferred by CDC in most clinical situations.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hand hygiene is still required after glove removal; rinsing with water alone is not an accepted method.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Non-alcohol-based waterless antiseptic agents are not recommended for hand hygiene in health-care settings.

items.stem: A nurse finishes care for a client with laboratory-confirmed Clostridioides difficile infection, removes gloves and gown, and finds a dedicated hand-washing sink immediately available. Hands are not visibly soiled. Which hand-hygiene method is preferred in this situation?

options.text: Apply alcohol-based hand rub only, because hands are not visibly soiled.
Wash with soap and water at the dedicated sink.
Wash with soap and water at the client's bathroom sink for convenience.
Skip hand hygiene because Contact Precautions gloves already protected the hands.

rationales.A: Incorrect. For C. difficile, soap and water is theoretically more effective at removing spores than alcohol-based hand rub when a dedicated sink is available.
rationales.B: Correct. PIDAC advises that when C. difficile is diagnosed or suspected and a dedicated hand-washing sink is immediately available, hands should be washed with soap and water. CDC likewise recommends soap and water during care of clients with C. difficile in outbreak settings.
rationales.C: Incorrect. PIDAC specifically advises not to perform hand hygiene at the client's sink because that may re-contaminate the health-care provider's hands.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Meticulous hand hygiene is required after glove removal; gloves do not replace hand hygiene.

items.jurisdiction_note: PIDAC prefers soap/water when a dedicated sink is available for C. difficile; if no dedicated sink, ABHR is used. The stem specifies a dedicated sink so the Canada-preferred action is keyed.

items.stem: During a skin assessment, the nurse finds intact skin over a client's sacral bony prominence with a localized area of nonblanchable erythema. Sensation over the area is slightly increased compared with surrounding skin. How should this finding be documented?

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury
Stage 2 pressure injury
Unstageable pressure injury
Deep-tissue pressure injury

rationales.A: Correct. Stage 1 is intact skin with localized nonblanchable erythema, often over a bony prominence; changes in sensation, temperature, or firmness may accompany it.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Stage 2 involves partial-thickness skin loss (shallow open ulcer or blister) with a pink/red wound bed, not intact skin alone.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Unstageable injuries have full-thickness loss obscured by slough or eschar so depth cannot be determined.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Deep-tissue pressure injury presents as persistent nonblanchable deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration, not simple nonblanchable erythema of Stage 1.

items.stem: A client is confined to bed after major abdominal surgery and is assessed as high risk for pressure injury. Which repositioning schedule best reflects evidence-based pressure-reduction practice?

options.text: Turn the client at least every 2 hours using a written schedule.
Turn the client once every 8-hour shift if the skin remains intact.
Keep the client supine continuously for the first 24 postoperative hours.
Reposition only when the client requests a position change.

rationales.A: Correct. Frequent repositioning is the most important pressure-reduction factor; bed-confined clients should be turned at least every 2 hours with a written schedule to direct and document the turns.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Waiting until every 8 hours is far less frequent than the minimum every-2-hour turning recommended for bed-confined clients.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Continuous supine positioning increases pressure-injury risk; early and scheduled repositioning is needed.
rationales.D: Incorrect. High-risk clients need a scheduled repositioning plan; relying only on client request is insufficient.

items.topic: Pressure injury prevention — repositioning schedule

sources.evidence: Frequent repositioning most important; written schedule; bed patients turned minimum every 2 hours.

items.stem: An adult with type 1 diabetes is admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis. Intravenous 0.9% saline has been started. The first serum potassium result is 3.0 mmol/L (3.0 mEq/L). Which action regarding insulin therapy is appropriate at this time?

options.text: Begin regular insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h IV immediately to correct the acidosis.
Withhold insulin temporarily, replace potassium, and start insulin once potassium is at least 3.3 mmol/L.
Give subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin only; intravenous insulin is not used in adult DKA.
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate first; insulin is unnecessary if bicarbonate is corrected.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Starting insulin while potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L risks dangerous further hypokalemia because insulin drives potassium into cells.
rationales.B: Correct. If serum potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L, insulin is withheld (or stopped) while potassium is replaced until potassium is at least 3.3 mmol/L. Diabetes Canada also emphasizes fluid resuscitation, avoidance of hypokalemia, and insulin as core DKA principles.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Adult DKA requires intravenous insulin (Diabetes Canada: 0.1 units/kg/h) for resolution; subcutaneous-only regimens are not the standard emergency approach described here.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Bicarbonate is considered only for extreme acidosis (pH ≤7.0) and does not replace insulin therapy.

items.topic: DKA — withhold insulin if severe hypokalemia
items.jurisdiction_note: Diabetes Canada and Merck both prioritize potassium management with insulin in DKA; the <3.3 mmol/L hold threshold is stated explicitly in Merck.

items.stem: A client with heart failure takes digoxin daily and was recently started on furosemide. Which laboratory finding most increases the risk of digoxin toxicity?

options.text: Serum potassium 2.9 mmol/L (2.9 mEq/L)
Serum sodium 138 mmol/L (138 mEq/L)
Hemoglobin 128 g/L (12.8 g/dL)
Serum glucose 5.8 mmol/L (104 mg/dL)

rationales.A: Correct. Hypokalemia sensitizes the myocardium to digoxin so toxicity may occur even when the digoxin level is in the usual range. Potassium-depleting diuretics such as furosemide increase this risk.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A sodium of 138 mmol/L is within a typical reference interval and is not the classic precipitant of digoxin toxicity highlighted in labelling.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hemoglobin near 128 g/L does not specifically increase digoxin toxicity risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A glucose of 5.8 mmol/L is not a recognized precipitant of digoxin toxicity in the cited sources.

items.topic: Digoxin — hypokalemia increases toxicity risk

items.stem: Before giving the morning digoxin tablet, the nurse counts the client's apical pulse for 1 full minute and obtains 52 beats/min. The client is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.text: Administer the digoxin as scheduled because the client has no symptoms.
Withhold the digoxin and notify the health-care provider.
Give half the ordered dose and recheck the pulse in 30 minutes.
Crush the tablet and give it with a high-potassium food to prevent toxicity.

rationales.A: Incorrect. An apical rate under 60 beats/min is an indication to withhold digoxin pending provider guidance, even if the client currently feels well.
rationales.B: Correct. Nursing practice guidance is to assess the pulse for 1 minute and not administer digoxin if the heart rate is less than 60 beats/min. The Canadian monograph likewise notes that bradycardia related to digoxin may require temporary withdrawal and monitoring.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Nurses do not independently halve digoxin doses; the dose should be withheld and the provider notified.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Crushing is not indicated solely for a low pulse, and giving the dose despite bradycardia is unsafe.

items.stem: A client with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation is started on warfarin for stroke prevention. The nurse reinforces teaching about the usual therapeutic INR target range for this indication. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: My INR goal is usually about 2.0 to 3.0.
My INR should stay below 1.0 at all times.
An INR above 5.0 is ideal for preventing clots.
Warfarin does not require blood-test monitoring once I feel well.

rationales.A: Correct. For most treatment durations, including atrial fibrillation, the Canadian product monograph targets an INR of 2.5 (range 2.0 to 3.0). OpenStax likewise cites a usual therapeutic INR of about 2–3.
rationales.B: Incorrect. An INR near or below 1.0 reflects little anticoagulant effect and does not meet the therapeutic target for atrial fibrillation.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Higher intensity anticoagulation increases bleeding risk; the monograph notes INR values greater than 4.0 provide little added benefit and raise bleeding risk for most patients.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Warfarin dosing is adjusted according to PT/INR results and requires ongoing monitoring.

items.stem: Fifteen minutes after starting a packed red blood cell transfusion, a client reports chills and new flank pain. Temperature has risen from 36.8°C to 38.2°C. After the nurse stops the transfusion, which concurrent action is most appropriate?

Keep the intravenous line open with normal saline using new tubing, and notify the blood bank.
Restart the same unit at a slower rate after giving acetaminophen.

items.stem: A postoperative client has brisk wound drainage into a surgical drain. The client is anxious. Capillary refill is delayed, skin is cool and clammy, heart rate is 118 beats/min, and blood pressure is 118/78 mm Hg. Which interpretation best fits these findings?

options.text: Early compensatory response to hypovolemia; tachycardia can precede frank hypotension.
Cardiogenic shock is most likely because blood pressure is still near the client's baseline.
Findings are reassuring; hypovolemic shock is excluded until systolic blood pressure falls below 90 mm Hg.
Neurogenic shock is most likely because the client is anxious after surgery.

rationales.A: Correct. In early hypovolemic compensation, sympathetic activation raises heart rate and vascular tone; blood pressure may remain normal or only slightly changed while tachycardia, cool clammy skin, and anxiety appear.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Cardiogenic shock involves pump failure; this picture of volume loss with compensatory tachycardia fits hypovolemia, not a primary cardiac pump problem.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hypotension is common in shock but is not required early; clients may be normotensive while compensation is still effective.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Neurogenic shock typically features bradycardia and warm dry skin from loss of sympathetic tone, not compensatory tachycardia with cool clammy skin.

items.stem: A client receiving a loop diuretic reports new muscle weakness and cramps. Serum potassium is 2.7 mmol/L (2.7 mEq/L). Which nursing action is the priority?

rationales.C: Incorrect. Loop diuretics increase urinary potassium loss and would worsen hypokalemia; the diuretic should not be given until the provider reassesses.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Dietary potassium is usually increased, not withheld, when treating hypokalemia unless the provider directs otherwise.

items.stem: A hospitalized adult with decreased level of consciousness is at risk for aspiration. Which nursing action best reduces aspiration risk during care?

options.text: Keep the client flat in a fully supine position for all oral care and feeding attempts.
Elevate the head of the bed to greater than 30 degrees (semi-upright) unless contraindicated, and avoid oral intake while consciousness is decreased.

items.stem: An immobile client after a stroke has flaccid extremities and cannot participate in active exercise. Which nursing intervention best helps prevent joint contractures?

Ask the spouse to override the client’s refusal and sign consent.

items.stem: Which nursing action is the most effective strategy to prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) in a hospitalized adult?

Avoid unnecessary catheterization and remove the indwelling catheter as soon as it is no longer needed.

items.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease has a serum potassium of 6.4 mmol/L (6.4 mEq/L). Which electrocardiogram (ECG) change is most consistent with hyperkalemia?

Shortened PR interval with no T-wave changes

items.stem: An immobile hospitalized adult is at high risk for pressure injury. Which nursing intervention best reduces pressure-related tissue injury risk?

Contact Precautions only, because measles never spreads through the air.

items.stem: Under Ontario’s Health Care Consent Act and CNO Consent guidance, which statement about decision-making capacity is accurate?

Only a court can ever determine that a person is capable of consenting to treatment.

Skip Tdap in pregnancy if a dose was given 2 years ago for a tetanus booster
Tdap is never given in pregnancy; wait until the child is 5 years old
Only the newborn needs vaccination at birth for pertussis; maternal Tdap is unnecessary

rationales.A: Correct. CDC and Merck: give a single Tdap during every pregnancy, preferably in the early part of gestational weeks 27–36, regardless of the interval since prior Tdap.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Additional Tdap is recommended each pregnancy regardless of interval since the previous dose (CDC/Merck).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Tdap in pregnancy is specifically recommended to protect infants (CDC/Merck).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Maternal vaccination in pregnancy is recommended to transfer antibodies; infants begin DTaP later in infancy, not a birth pertussis dose as the sole strategy.

items.stem: A client begins to disclose a painful personal experience. The nurse feels uncomfortable and quickly asks about the weather instead. Which evaluation of this response is accurate?

options.text: Changing the subject is a nontherapeutic barrier that can seem insensitive and shut down disclosure
Changing the subject is the preferred therapeutic technique for painful topics
Changing the subject always increases trust more than active listening
Nurses should change the subject whenever clients show emotion

rationales.C: Incorrect. Active listening supports trust; changing the subject undermines it.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Emotional disclosure is a cue to stay present therapeutically, not to divert.

items.stem: A client with schizophrenia firmly believes hospital food is poisoned despite evidence to the contrary. After safety is assured, which nursing communication approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Establish trust with therapeutic communication, then help the client focus on reality-based themes rather than arguing about the delusion
Agree that the food is poisoned to build rapport
Loudly argue until the client retracts the belief
Ignore the client and withhold all meals indefinitely

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: for clients experiencing delusions, establish therapeutic communication and trust, then help focus on reality-based themes. Merck: delusions are erroneous beliefs maintained despite clear contradictory evidence — arguing facts alone rarely erases the belief; supportive, reality-oriented psychosocial care is part of treatment.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Reinforcing a delusion is not therapeutic and can worsen safety planning.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Confrontational arguing is nontherapeutic and may escalate distress.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Withholding meals is harmful and unrelated to therapeutic communication.

items.stem: A 5-week-old infant has forceful, nonbilious vomiting after feeds, still seems hungry, and has a firm olive-like mass in the right epigastrium. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
Uncomplicated physiologic gastroesophageal reflux with bilious emesis only
Typical viral gastroenteritis with predominantly watery diarrhea and no vomiting
Simple overfeeding without gastric outlet obstruction risk

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis typically presents at 3–6 weeks with forceful/projectile nonbilious emesis after eating; an olive-like pyloric mass may be palpable. NCBI StatPearls physiology text: IHPS presents with projectile nonbilious vomiting and a palpable olive; definitive treatment is pyloromyotomy after fluid/electrolyte correction.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Classic pyloric stenosis emesis is nonbilious; bilious vomiting suggests a different obstruction pattern.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The vignette centres on postprandial projectile vomiting and an olive mass, not diarrhea-predominant gastroenteritis.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting with an olive mass indicates gastric outlet obstruction needing evaluation, not simple overfeeding.

items.stem: A public health nurse teaches daycare staff how to limit spread of hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wash hands often with soap and water, especially after diaper changes and toileting
Clean and disinfect frequently touched surfaces and shared toys
Avoid close contact such as hugging or kissing persons who are infected
Rely on a routinely available HFMD vaccine in Canada/US as the primary prevention method
Avoid contact with open skin lesions and oral secretions (drool) when caring for ill children

items.stem: A 4-week-old has projectile nonbilious vomiting, remains eager to feed, and has a palpable olive-like epigastric mass. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Uncomplicated lactose intolerance without obstruction
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
Acute appendicitis
Simple overfeeding only

actions.text: Support airway/breathing as needed and keep NPO pending surgical evaluation
Correct dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities with IV fluids as ordered before surgery
Encourage unlimited formula immediately before emergent laparotomy without fluid resuscitation
Prepare for pyloromyotomy after medical stabilization as ordered
Discharge home without evaluation because vomiting is always normal at this age

parameters.text: Hydration status and urine output
Serum electrolytes (watch for hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis)
Stock market indices
Unrelated school grades of siblings
Weight trend / ongoing vomiting frequency

rationales.K1: Incorrect. Lactose intolerance does not produce an olive-like pyloric mass with classic projectile nonbilious pattern of IHPS.
rationales.K2: Correct. Merck/NCBI: IHPS — projectile nonbilious vomiting in early weeks with possible olive mass.
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Appendicitis is not the classic 3–6 week olive-mass presentation.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Progressive projectile vomiting with olive mass is not simple overfeeding.
rationales.A1: Incorrect. While NPO pending evaluation may occur, the sourced priority actions are fluid/electrolyte correction and pyloromyotomy after stabilization.
rationales.A2: Correct. Merck: correct dehydration and electrolyte/acid-base abnormalities before pyloromyotomy.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Feeding without correcting fluids/electrolytes and rushing without stabilization is unsafe.
rationales.A4: Correct. Definitive treatment is pyloromyotomy after medical stabilization (Merck/NCBI).
rationales.A5: Incorrect. This presentation requires prompt evaluation, not casual discharge.
rationales.P1: Correct. Dehydration risk is central; monitor hydration/urine output (Merck).
rationales.P2: Correct. Classic abnormality is hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (Merck/NCBI).
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Irrelevant parameter.
rationales.P5: Plausible monitoring but not selected as a keyed parameter for this item; electrolytes and hydration are the highest-yield sourced parameters.

items.stem: A capable adult client asks an Ontario nurse for a romantic and sexual relationship while still receiving nursing care. Which response meets CNO accountabilities?

options.text: Decline; any sexual relationship with a current client is sexual abuse and is never permissible
Accept if the client signs a consent form agreeing to the relationship
Accept after work hours because off-duty contact is not regulated
Accept if the nurse feels mutual attraction and documents it in the chart

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: any sexual relationship with a patient is sexual abuse; there is no circumstance in which sexual interaction between a nurse and a patient is permissible. OpenStax: therapeutic relationships are never sexual.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Client agreement does not make a sexual relationship permissible under CNO/RHPA sexual-abuse rules.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Boundary and sexual-abuse accountabilities apply regardless of on- or off-duty timing while the therapeutic relationship exists (and for a defined period after).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Attraction or charting does not authorize a sexual or romantic relationship with a client.

items.stem: A home-care client offers an Ontario nurse an expensive personal gift of jewellery. Which action best maintains professional boundaries?

options.text: Decline the valuable personal gift; avoid gift exchange that blurs boundaries, and do not solicit gifts
Accept the jewellery if the client insists it is a thank-you
Accept the gift and give the client preferential visiting times in return
Ask the client’s family for a matching gift so the exchange feels fair

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: nurses should avoid giving and accepting gifts that blur boundaries; gifts should never have more than token value and must not be solicited. OpenStax: therapeutic relationships are not social relationships in which personal exchanges meet the nurse’s needs.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Client insistence does not authorize accepting a valuable personal gift that risks conflict of interest and altered clinical judgment (CNO).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Preferential treatment in return for a gift is a boundary violation and conflict of interest.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Soliciting or expanding gift exchange worsens the boundary breach (CNO: do not solicit gifts).

items.stem: Complete the cloze describing TeamSTEPPS check-back (closed-loop) communication for a verbal medication order.

ngn.template: In TeamSTEPPS check-back, the {B1} initiates the message (for example, a verbal order). The {B2} accepts the message and provides feedback by repeating it. Then the original sender {B3} that the message was received as intended (for example, 'That's correct').

B1.text: medical records clerk with no role in the order

B3.text: changes the dose silently without speaking
leaves the unit immediately without verifying

rationales.B1b: Correct. AHRQ/Pocket Guide: sender initiates the message.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. An uninvolved bystander is not the sender.

rationales.B2a: Correct. Receiver accepts the message and provides feedback (repeat-back).
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Check-back requires human closed-loop verification as described in TeamSTEPPS.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. A hallway visitor is not the clinical message receiver.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Social media is not part of TeamSTEPPS check-back.
rationales.B3a: Incorrect. Closing the loop requires sender confirmation.
rationales.B3b: Correct. Sender double-checks to ensure the message was received as intended.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Silent dose changes without verification defeat closed-loop safety.
rationales.B3d: Incorrect. Leaving without verification fails closed-loop communication.

items.stem: A charge nurse must give formative feedback after a teammate omitted a safety check. Which approach best matches TeamSTEPPS mutual-support guidance?

options.text: Give timely, respectful, behaviour-specific feedback directed toward improvement, preferably privately for negative feedback
Wait several weeks so emotions cool, then criticize the teammate’s personality in front of the whole unit
Assume the teammate is lazy and announce that judgment at the nursing station
Never give feedback unless you are the formal manager doing an annual evaluation

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS: formative feedback should be timely, respectful (behaviour not personality), specific, directed toward improvement, and considerate; negative feedback should not be given in front of other team members.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Delayed, personality-focused, public criticism violates timely/respectful/private guidance.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Attributing poor performance to internal traits (lazy) and public shaming undermine mutual support.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Any team member can give formative feedback; it is not limited to formal leaders or annual reviews.

items.stem: During a scheduled Ontario virtual visit, the nurse determines the client’s condition requires a hands-on physical assessment that cannot be completed virtually. Which action is most appropriate?

Continue the video visit only and document that virtual care is always sufficient
End the call without arranging any alternative care pathway

items.stem: An 84-year-old develops new fluctuating confusion over 24 hours with marked inattention after a UTI. Which interpretation best distinguishes this presentation from typical dementia?

options.text: Acute onset with fluctuating course and impaired attention suggests delirium and needs urgent evaluation of causes
Any confusion in older adults is dementia and never reversible
Sudden fluctuating confusion always means Alzheimer disease beginning overnight
Delirium never occurs in clients who also have dementia

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: delirium has sudden onset, fluctuating course, mainly impaired attention, often reversible when the cause is treated. OpenStax: delirium starts suddenly over hours to days and often comes and goes.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Mistaking delirium for dementia is a common error; delirium is often reversible (Merck).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Dementia/major NCD is typically gradual and progressive, not overnight (Merck/OpenStax).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Delirium commonly occurs superimposed on dementia (Merck).

items.stem: An older adult with recurrent aspiration risk is receiving nursing care. Besides positioning and swallow strategies, which comfort/hygiene intervention helps reduce aspiration pneumonia risk?

options.text: Optimize oral hygiene (for example, assisted toothbrushing/denture care) to reduce harmful oral bacteria
Stop all oral care because moisture always increases aspiration
Keep the mouth colonized intentionally to 'train' immunity
Replace oral care with routine application of petroleum products into the airway

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: optimizing oral hygiene may help prevent pneumonia/abscess in patients who repeatedly aspirate. OpenStax: improve oral hygiene and assist with toothbrushing/denture care to decrease harmful oral bacteria.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Oral care is a prevention strategy, not something to eliminate solely for aspiration risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Colonization with oral pathogens increases pneumonia risk after aspiration.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Putting petroleum products into the airway is unsafe and not an oral-hygiene strategy.

items.stem: An older adult develops sudden fluctuating confusion and inattention over 18 hours during hospitalization for pneumonia. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Typical slow-onset Alzheimer dementia as the sole explanation
Delirium (acute confusional state), often secondary to acute illness
Uncomplicated loneliness without cognitive change
Stable lifelong intellectual disability without acute change

actions.text: Urgently evaluate and treat reversible contributors (e.g., infection, medications, metabolic issues) while supporting safety
Provide a calm supportive environment; avoid restraints when possible
Assume the change is permanent dementia and cancel medical workup
Discharge immediately without assessing causes of acute confusion
Start high-dose recreational sedatives without clinical assessment

parameters.text: Mental status / attention and fluctuation pattern
Vital signs and clinical indicators of the precipitating illness
Stock ticker symbols
Unrelated celebrity news headlines
Fashion trends on social media

rationales.K1: Incorrect. Overnight fluctuating confusion is not explained solely as typical gradual Alzheimer dementia (Merck/OpenStax).
rationales.K2: Correct. Sudden fluctuating confusion with inattention is delirium, often from acute illness (Merck/OpenStax).
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Marked acute cognitive change is not uncomplicated loneliness.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. A new acute change is not a stable lifelong disability pattern.
rationales.A1: Correct. Delirium management centres on identifying/treating underlying causes; needs immediate attention (Merck/OpenStax).
rationales.A2: Correct. OpenStax: supportive environment; avoid restraints. Merck: treat underlying condition.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Cancelling workup risks missing reversible causes.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Acute delirium requires evaluation, not casual discharge.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Unassessed sedatives can worsen delirium and are unsafe.
rationales.P1: Correct. Track mental status/attention and fluctuation (core delirium features).
rationales.P2: Correct. Monitor vitals/illness indicators tied to precipitants (e.g., infection).
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Irrelevant parameter.

Confront the colleague loudly in front of the client so others witness accountability
Ignore the behaviour because interpersonal conflict never affects patient safety

rationales.D: Incorrect. Social-media airing is not a TeamSTEPPS conflict-resolution method and breaches professionalism.

Continue full independent practice while keeping the health issue secret from all supports
Use alcohol at work to steady nerves so clients are unaware

items.stem: A client with contamination obsessions and washing compulsions begins evidence-based psychotherapy. Which treatment element is essential?

options.text: Gradual exposure to anxiety triggers while preventing the usual compulsive ritual (exposure and response prevention)
Encouraging longer and more frequent washing until anxiety disappears permanently
Arguing that the client’s obsessions are deliberately invented for attention

rationales.D: Incorrect. Insight varies; education and collaborative ERP are standard.

items.stem: A client who abruptly stopped long-term opioid use has yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, and piloerection. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Findings fit opioid withdrawal; assess with a validated scale (e.g., COWS) and manage symptoms
Findings fit opioid overdose; the priority is that pupils are always pinpoint
Opioid withdrawal is usually immediately life-threatening like status epilepticus and needs deep sedation first
These autonomic signs only occur with alcohol withdrawal, never opioid withdrawal

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: mydriasis, piloerection, lacrimation/rhinorrhea, and yawning are specific opioid-withdrawal signs. OpenStax: use COWS/CINA and focus on symptom management in withdrawal.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Overdose triad includes pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression (OpenStax); mydriasis fits withdrawal more than typical overdose.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Merck: opioid withdrawal is distressingly symptomatic but not itself typically life-threatening.
rationales.D: Incorrect. These signs are described for opioid withdrawal (Merck).

items.stem: A client 24 hours after stopping heroin has anxiety, yawning, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, gooseflesh, and abdominal cramps. Complete the bowtie.

conditions.text: Opioid overdose with respiratory depression
Opioid withdrawal
Serotonin syndrome
Hypoglycemia alone

actions.text: Assess withdrawal severity with a validated scale (e.g., COWS) and provide ordered symptom-focused care
Administer high-dose naloxone repeatedly as the only intervention for these findings
Supportive monitoring and anticipate agonist/partial-agonist therapy (e.g., methadone or buprenorphine) per protocol
Encourage immediate unsupervised return to street opioid use to “self-treat”
Ignore autonomic signs because withdrawal never needs nursing assessment

parameters.text: Vital signs and withdrawal symptom trend
Hydration and gastrointestinal symptom control
Pupil size only once at admission with no reassessment
Whether the client can leave without any safety or follow-up plan
Response to ordered medications for withdrawal symptoms

rationales.K1: Incorrect. Overdose features respiratory depression/pinpoint pupils; this vignette matches withdrawal.
rationales.K2: Correct. Yawning, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, piloerection, cramps fit opioid withdrawal (Merck).
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome is a different toxidrome not supported by this cue set.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Hypoglycemia alone does not explain this autonomic cluster.
rationales.A1: Correct. OpenStax: assess with COWS and manage symptoms.
rationales.A2: Incorrect. Naloxone is for overdose/respiratory depression, not first-line for this withdrawal picture.
rationales.A3: Correct. Merck: substitution with methadone or buprenorphine plus supportive care.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Unsupervised return to use is unsafe and not treatment.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Withdrawal requires assessment and supportive management.
rationales.P1: Correct. Trend vital signs and withdrawal symptoms to guide care.
rationales.P2: Incorrect. Although GI comfort matters, the keyed monitoring priorities here are vital/withdrawal trends and medication response.
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Single unchecked pupil assessment is inadequate monitoring.
rationales.P4: Incorrect. Discharge without plan is unsafe.
rationales.P5: Correct. Monitor response to ordered withdrawal medications.

conditions.text: Thyroid storm
Myxedema coma
Adrenal crisis from abrupt steroid withdrawal only
Serotonin syndrome

Give glucocorticoids as ordered while adrenal insufficiency is not yet excluded
Rapidly rewarm with aggressive external heating to reverse hypotension
Start high-dose oral methimazole immediately as first-line therapy

rationales.P2: Correct. Respiratory depression/CO2 retention and hypoxemia require ventilation/PaO2 monitoring (Merck/OpenStax).

items.stem: An Ontario RN is assisting a nurse practitioner who is providing medical assistance in dying (MAID). Which action is within the RN’s legal role?

options.text: Insert an intravenous line with an order for later use by the NP/physician administering MAID medications
Personally administer the medications that will cause the client’s death
Independently determine MAID eligibility and write the MAID medication order
Pressure the client to choose MAID to free a hospital bed

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: RNs/RPNs may assist by activities such as inserting an IV line (with an order) that will be used to administer MAID medications; only NPs and physicians may administer those medications.
rationales.B: Incorrect. CNO: only NPs and physicians may administer medications to cause death for practitioner-assisted MAID; RNs/RPNs are not permitted to administer them.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Eligibility assessment/administration authority is limited to NPs and physicians.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CNO: nurses giving information must not encourage or pressure the client to choose MAID.

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO conscientious objection rules for MAID participation.
items.topic: Ontario MAID conscientious objection — transfer care; continue unrelated care; do not convey objection to client
items.stem: An Ontario nurse conscientiously objects to participating in MAID for an assigned client. What is the correct next action?

options.text: Transfer care to another appropriate provider and continue other nursing care unrelated to MAID until replacement is arranged, without expressing moral judgment to the client
Tell the client that choosing MAID is morally wrong and refuse all care immediately
Abandon the client without arranging alternate care
Administer the MAID medications personally despite the objection

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: conscientious objection must not be directly conveyed to the patient; transfer care to another nurse/provider; continue other nursing care unrelated to MAID until a replacement is found.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Objection must not be conveyed; moral judgments about the client must not be expressed; unrelated care continues until transfer.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Care must be transferred appropriately; abandonment is not permitted.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Objection means the nurse does not provide/assist MAID activities; administration is also outside RN authority.

items.topic: Neonatal phototherapy — diaper only + eye protection; monitor temperature

options.text: Place the infant under the lights wearing only a diaper with eye patches/mask in place, and monitor temperature frequently
Dress the infant in a heavy sleeper and leave the eyes uncovered for bonding under the lights
Cover the infant completely with blankets so no skin is exposed to the light
Skip temperature checks because phototherapy cannot affect body temperature

items.topic: Home oxygen safety — no smoking; keep away from open flame/heat; avoid petroleum-based lotions
items.stem: The nurse teaches a client starting home oxygen therapy. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Do not smoke or allow smoking near oxygen; keep oxygen away from open flames/heat sources; avoid petroleum-based lotions on the face or upper body
Smoking is safe if the oxygen flow is turned down to 1 L/min
Petroleum jelly is preferred on the nose and face while oxygen is in use
Place oxygen equipment next to a wood stove to warm the gas before use

rationales.B: Incorrect. Smoking near oxygen is prohibited regardless of flow rate.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Petroleum-based products are discouraged; water-based preferred.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Keep oxygen away from open flames/heat.

items.topic: Insulin injection — rotate sites; avoid repeated use of lumpy sites

Always inject into the exact same abdominal spot for consistent absorption
Inject only into bruised areas so healing tissue absorbs insulin faster

items.topic: IV infiltration — cool swollen site; stop infusion and remove catheter
items.stem: A peripheral IV site is swollen and cool to the touch, and the client reports pain at the site. What is the priority nursing action?

Increase the infusion rate to clear the swelling
Ignore the findings if the pump is not alarming
Flush forcefully with 20 mL of undiluted potassium chloride

items.topic: Acute mania — calm clear communication; do not challenge grandiosity; prioritize safety
items.stem: A client in acute mania is agitated, speaking rapidly, and making grandiose plans to leave against advice. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Use a calm demeanor, give concise clear directions, avoid arguing about grandiose ideas, and prioritize a safe environment
Loudly debate each grandiose claim until the client admits they are false
Encourage a large stimulating group activity to burn off energy
Leave the client unsupervised in a crowded waiting area

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: during manic phases maintain a calm demeanor, provide concise clear directions, avoid challenging grandiosity, and ensure a safe environment. Merck: manic episodes involve severe impairment/risky behavior that may require hospitalization — safety is priority.

rationales.C: Incorrect. High stimulation is counterproductive in acute mania.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Safety requires supervision/structured environment.

items.topic: NGN bowtie — acute dystonia from antipsychotic: recognize and treat with benztropine/diphenhydramine
items.stem: A client who recently started a first-generation antipsychotic develops sudden torticollis and tongue spasms. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Tardive dyskinesia only (late irreversible choreiform movements)
Acute dystonic reaction (extrapyramidal)
Serotonin syndrome
Hypoglycemic seizure

actions.text: Notify the provider and administer benztropine or diphenhydramine as ordered (IV/IM)
Hold further doses of the causative antipsychotic pending provider guidance
Encourage the client to ignore the spasms and continue the same antipsychotic dose without assessment
Start a high-dose SSRI immediately as first-line therapy for the spasms
Force oral intake of a large high-carbohydrate meal as the only intervention

parameters.text: Airway patency and ability to swallow/speak (watch for laryngeal involvement)
Resolution of muscle spasms / dystonic movements after treatment
Peak expiratory flow only as the sole monitoring plan
Urine specific gravity every minute without neuromuscular assessment
Orthostatic blood pressure after sprint exercise only

rationales.K1: Incorrect. Tardive dyskinesia is a late effect, not the acute spasmodic torticollis/tongue spasm picture.
rationales.K2: Correct. OpenStax: dystonia includes spasms of tongue, back, legs, neck — an EPS of antipsychotics. Merck: acute dystonic reactions (e.g., torticollis, oculogyric crisis).
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome is a different toxidrome.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Not a hypoglycemic presentation.
rationales.A1: Correct. Merck: treat acute dystonia with benztropine IV/IM or diphenhydramine IV/IM.
rationales.A2: Correct. OpenStax/Merck: monitor EPS so treatment can be given and antipsychotic regimen adjusted/changed.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Acute dystonia requires prompt treatment.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. SSRIs are not treatment for dystonia.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Not the antidote pathway.
rationales.P1: Correct. Merck notes laryngeal dystonia may threaten airway.
rationales.P2: Correct. Reassess spasm resolution after anticholinergic/antihistamine therapy.
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Peak flow alone misses airway/neuromuscular priorities.
rationales.P5: Incorrect. Not priority monitoring for acute dystonia.

items.topic: PTSD flashback — ground in present (senses/here-and-now); reassure safety
items.stem: A client with PTSD suddenly appears terrified, stares past the nurse, and seems to be re-experiencing a past assault. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.text: Calmly orient the client to the present using grounding (e.g., what they can see/hear/touch now) and reassure that they are safe
Insist the client immediately recount every detail of the trauma aloud
Leave the client alone in a dark room until the episode ends
Argue that the trauma never happened and demand they 'snap out of it'

Trauma flashback / acute re-experiencing (PTSD)

Benign positional vertigo

items.topic: Ontario LTC — nurse must report suspected resident abuse/neglect (FLTCA / CNO)
items.stem: An Ontario RN working in a long-term care home has reasonable grounds to suspect that a resident was abused by a staff member and that the resident was harmed. Which action meets legal and professional accountabilities?

options.text: Immediately report the suspicion through the required LTC reporting pathway (to the Director / designated reporting line) — confidentiality does not excuse failing to report
Wait several weeks to see whether the resident complains formally before taking any action
Keep the information confidential and tell no one because of PHIPA
Confront the alleged abuser privately and close the matter without any report

rationales.C: Incorrect. Mandatory reporting duties override ordinary confidentiality in this setting.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Informal confrontation without required reporting does not meet FLTCA/CNO accountabilities.

Set the handle at shoulder height so the elbow is locked straight
Set the handle below the knee so the client must lean far forward

items.topic: Cane on stairs — up with stronger leg first; down with weaker/injured leg first
items.stem: The nurse teaches stair safety with a cane after right ankle surgery. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Going up, step up with the stronger (uninjured) leg first; going down, lead with the cane and the weaker/injured leg, then the stronger leg
Always lead with the injured leg when going up and down
Carry the cane and hop on the injured leg without using a handrail when available
Place both feet on each step before moving the cane, ignoring which leg is stronger

rationales.B: Incorrect. Leading with the injured leg when ascending is unsafe.
rationales.C: Incorrect. AAOS: use free hand on handrail when available; do not hop on injured leg.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Sequence depends on stronger vs weaker leg for ascent and descent.

items.topic: Therapeutic communication — prefer open-ended invitation; avoid accusatory why questions
items.stem: A client says, "I feel like everything is falling apart." Which nurse response best uses therapeutic communication?

options.text: "Tell me more about what has been going on for you."
"Why did you let things get this bad?"
"At least you are not as sick as some other people here."
"You should just stop worrying and think positive."

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: open-ended questions support therapeutic communication. OpenStax PMH: explore with open-ended questions rather than accusatory why or minimizing remarks.
rationales.B: Incorrect. OpenStax PMH: asking why can imply accusation/judgment and provoke defensiveness.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Minimizing remarks belittle the client's feelings.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Advice-giving/false positivity is nontherapeutic compared with open exploration.

items.topic: Just culture — system issues + accountability; blame-free reporting of human error/near misses; zero tolerance for reckless behaviour

items.topic: Fifth disease (parvovirus B19) — usually return to school after slapped-cheek rash appears
items.stem: A school-age child develops the bright "slapped cheek" rash of fifth disease (parvovirus B19) after a few days of mild cold symptoms and is now afebrile. Which teaching is most accurate about contagiousness and school attendance?

The rash means the child is most contagious and must be isolated in a negative-pressure room at school

rationales.D: Incorrect. Human parvovirus B19 spreads person to person (respiratory/blood); pet parvoviruses are different.

items.topic: Metformin — hold around IV iodinated contrast; lactic acidosis risk
items.stem: A client taking metformin is scheduled for a radiologic procedure with IV iodinated contrast. Which teaching is most accurate?

items.topic: ECT — controlled seizure under anesthesia; temporary memory impairment possible
items.stem: A client with severe treatment-resistant depression is scheduled for ECT. Which teaching is most accurate?

options.text: ECT induces a controlled seizure under anesthesia/supportive care and may cause temporary confusion or memory impairment that often improves over time

ECT permanently erases all remote and recent memory in every client and is never used for depression
ECT replaces the need for any consent discussion because it is only a psychotherapy technique

items.topic: Ontario — nurse must report suspected sexual abuse of a patient by a nurse to CNO
items.stem: An Ontario nurse hears a patient's credible account that another nurse touched them in a sexual manner during care. What is the reporting obligation?

options.text: Report the suspected sexual abuse to the College of Nurses of Ontario (CNO) as required; a patient's account can constitute reasonable grounds
Wait indefinitely until a criminal conviction is obtained before any report is considered
Ignore the disclosure because consensual-appearing relationships with current patients are allowed
Post the patient's name and details on social media to warn the public

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: nurses are legally required to report suspected sexual abuse of a patient by a nurse to CNO. rationales.B: Incorrect. Reporting obligation does not wait for criminal conviction; report suspected sexual abuse promptly (within RHPA timelines).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Any sexual/romantic relationship with a patient is sexual abuse for regulated health professionals.
rationales.D: Incorrect. PHI must not be posted publicly; patient name in a CNO report requires written consent.

options.text: Have the person wear an ID/medical bracelet (or necklace) with name, address/phone, and caregiver contact information
Leave car keys in plain sight by the door so the person can drive home independently
Remove all door/window alarms because they are too noisy
Avoid telling neighbors about wandering risk to protect privacy completely

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: wear ID bracelet/necklace with name, address, phone, and caretaker contact. NIA: medical bracelet with name/address and caregiver phone number; label clothes if bracelet may be removed.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Keep car keys out of sight to reduce unsafe departure.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Door/window alarms are recommended prevention supports.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Informing neighbors is recommended so they can help if wandering occurs.

items.topic: TED/compression stockings — smooth wrinkles; nonslip footwear when ambulating

Leave large wrinkles at the ankles because wrinkles improve compression
Walk freely in stocking feet on polished floors without nonslip footwear
Roll the top tightly as a tourniquet band to keep the stocking from slipping

items.topic: Therapeutic communication — using silence gives the client time to think and process
items.stem: A client pauses after saying, “I’m not sure I can talk about this yet.” Which nurse action best uses silence as a therapeutic communication technique?

options.text: Remain quiet and present, allowing the client time to think and break the silence when ready
Immediately fill the pause with advice about what the client should feel
Change the subject to unit visiting hours to lighten the mood
Say, “Don’t worry—everything will be fine,” and leave the room

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: using silence allows the patient time to think and process; nurses should respectfully let the patient break the silence. Open RN Fundamentals: providing silence gives clients time to process, self-reflect, and broach a new topic; the nurse may use nonverbal cues but does not rush to speak.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Filling silence with advice interrupts processing and can be nontherapeutic.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Changing the subject is a nontherapeutic barrier.
rationales.D: Incorrect. False reassurance and leaving abandon therapeutic presence.

sources.title: 2.3 Communicating With Patients

items.topic: Infant burping — gently pat/rub back during and after feeds to release trapped air
items.stem: Parents ask how to burp their newborn who fusses with gas during feeds. Which teaching is correct?

options.text: During and after feeding, hold the infant in a supported burping position and gently pat or rub the back to help release swallowed air
Pound firmly between the shoulder blades for several minutes every time, even if the baby is comfortable
Never burp bottle-fed or breastfed infants because burping always causes injury
Lay the infant completely flat and shake the torso to move air out of the stomach

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: burping removes trapped air; use shoulder/lap positions and gently rub or pat the back; breastfed often between breasts and at end; bottle-fed as needed during/after. MedlinePlus: burp several times during and after feeding with upright support and gentle patting.
rationales.B: Incorrect. OpenStax: do not pound harder—this can cause injury and does not improve burping.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Both breastfed and bottle-fed infants may swallow air and benefit from burping.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Supported upright/lap burping positions are taught; shaking is unsafe.

items.jurisdiction_note: Health Canada and Canadian Cancer Society SPF 30+ guidance (stricter than some US SPF 15 minima)
items.topic: Canada sun safety — broad-spectrum water-resistant sunscreen SPF 30+; reapply about every 2 hours
items.stem: A community nurse in Canada teaches outdoor workers about sunscreen. Which instruction matches Canadian public-health guidance?

options.text: Use a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and reapply at least every 2 hours (sooner if sweating/swimming)
Any lip balm without SPF fully replaces sunscreen for the face and body
Apply sunscreen once each spring and never reapply during outdoor work
Indoor tanning beds are a healthy way to build a protective base tan before summer

rationales.A: Correct. Health Canada: broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher; apply ≥15 minutes before sun; reapply at least every 2 hours and after sweating/swimming. Canadian Cancer Society: broad-spectrum SPF 30+; reapply every 2 hours or after sweating/swimming; use with shade/clothing/hats.
rationales.B: Incorrect. SPF lip balm protects lips but does not replace full-body sunscreen.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Reapplication at least every 2 hours during exposure is required.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Health Canada: avoid tanning equipment; no healthy tan; increases melanoma risk.

items.topic: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease — supportive care; antibiotics do not shorten the viral illness
items.stem: Parents of a toddler with hand, foot, and mouth disease ask for antibiotics “to clear it faster.” Which nurse response is best?

options.text: Antibiotics will not make this viral illness go away faster; focus on comfort, fluids, and fever/pain relief as directed, and hand hygiene to limit spread
Start leftover amoxicillin from a sibling’s ear infection today
Antibiotics are required for every child with HFMD to prevent lifelong carriage
Give aspirin every 4 hours until the rash disappears

rationales.A: Correct. CPS: no treatment for the infection; antibiotics won’t help it go away faster; comfort, fluids, acetaminophen/ibuprofen for mouth-sore pain; handwashing. CDC: usually get better in 7–10 days with minimal/no medical treatment; manage pain/fever; never give aspirin to children.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Leftover antibiotics are inappropriate for this viral illness and unsafe.
rationales.C: Incorrect. HFMD is viral; antibiotics are not routinely indicated.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC: never give aspirin to children (Reye risk context for viral illness).

items.topic: TeamSTEPPS DESC script — constructive approach for interpersonal/hostile conflict
items.stem: A colleague repeatedly humiliates a nurse in front of clients. Which TeamSTEPPS tool is most appropriate to manage this interpersonal conflict constructively?

options.text: Use the DESC script (Describe, Express, Suggest, Consequences) in a private, respectful conversation focused on win-win resolution
Ignore the behaviour indefinitely because conflict tools are only for medication orders
Yell the same insults back at the colleague in the hallway to “even the score”
Post the colleague’s name and complaints on social media for public shaming

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS DESC tool: constructive approach for managing/resolving conflict, especially interpersonal/hostile or harassing behaviours risking harm; use private location and “I” statements. CUSP/TeamSTEPPS notes: DESC = Describe, Express, Suggest, Consequences.
rationales.B: Incorrect. DESC is intended for conflict management, including interpersonal conflict affecting safety/teamwork.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Retaliatory public confrontation is not DESC and harms patients/team.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Public shaming is unprofessional and not a TeamSTEPPS conflict tool.

items.topic: CNO — do not abandon clients; arrange alternative/replacement services when discontinuing care
items.stem: An Ontario nurse plans to discontinue nursing services for a client who still needs care. Which action best meets CNO accountabilities?

options.text: Arrange timely alternative or replacement services, or give the client a reasonable opportunity to arrange them—do not abandon the client
Stop all care immediately without notice because the nurse is annoyed with the client
Walk away mid-shift without communicating with the client, team, or employer
Refuse to explore any options and leave the client without access to ongoing care

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Discontinuing or Declining to Provide Care: nurses cannot abandon/neglect clients; ensure ongoing access to care; discontinue only after other options explored. Code of Conduct 3.13: arrange timely alternative/replacement services or provide reasonable opportunity to arrange them. Professional misconduct regulation also addresses discontinuation without alternatives.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Annoyance alone is not a basis to abandon needed services without alternatives.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Clear communication with client/team/employer is required.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Exploring options and ensuring access to care are required.

items.topic: HFMD infection control — hand hygiene and stay home while symptomatic
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A daycare asks how to limit spread of hand, foot, and mouth disease. Which instruction is best?

options.text: Promote frequent handwashing with soap and water, clean/disinfect toys and surfaces, and keep symptomatic children home from daycare/school
Stop all handwashing because HFMD is not contagious
Encourage hugging and sharing drinks with children who have active mouth sores
Tell parents HFMD never spreads through saliva or stool

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: wash hands often, clean/disinfect surfaces, avoid close contact with infected persons. CPS: handwashing best prevention; wash toys/surfaces; children should stay home from school/child care if they have symptoms; spreads via saliva/stool.
rationales.B: Incorrect. HFMD is very contagious; hand hygiene is essential.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Avoid close contact/kissing/hugging while infectious; do not share fluids with mouth sores.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CPS/CDC: spreads through saliva/droplets and stool/contact with contaminated objects.

items.topic: IV potassium — never administer as IV push/bolus; use diluted infusion
items.stem: A provider orders IV potassium chloride for a hospitalized client with hypokalemia. Which nursing action is essential for safe administration?

options.text: Never give potassium as an IV push or bolus; administer only as a diluted IV infusion at a controlled rate
Push undiluted potassium chloride concentrate rapidly through a peripheral IV for fastest correction
Add concentrated potassium to a running IV and bolus the line without an infusion pump
Give the entire daily potassium deficit as a single undiluted IV push at the start of the shift

rationales.B: Incorrect. Undiluted IV push of potassium concentrate can be fatal.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Rapid uncontrolled bolus bypasses safe infusion controls.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Deficits are replaced with controlled infusion, not a single undiluted push.

items.topic: Disulfiram — avoid alcohol and alcohol-containing products; reaction risk persists after last dose
items.stem: A client starting disulfiram for alcohol use disorder asks what to avoid. Which teaching is most accurate?

options.text: Avoid alcoholic beverages and alcohol-containing products (e.g., some cough syrups/elixirs); unpleasant reactions can still occur for days after the last dose

rationales.D: Incorrect. Disulfiram must not be given during intoxication; wait ≥12 hours after drinking.

ngn.template: Under O. Reg. 799/93, directing a team member to perform nursing functions they are not {B1} to perform is {B2}. Before assigning a skilled task, the RN should verify {B3}.

B3.text: required education and competency for that task
only the staff member’s lunch preference
the color of the assignment board
whether visitors approve of the schedule

rationales.B1a: Correct. O. Reg. 799/93 item 3 uses ‘not adequately trained or … not competent’.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Overtime interest is not the regulatory standard.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Irrelevant.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Irrelevant.
rationales.B2a: Correct. The regulation defines this directing as professional misconduct.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. It is misconduct, not a bonus criterion.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Not related to breaks.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. It is explicitly in the nursing misconduct regulation.
rationales.B3a: Correct. OpenStax Right Person: verify education and competencies.
rationales.B3b: Incorrect. Lunch preference is not competency verification.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Irrelevant.
rationales.B3d: Incorrect. Visitor approval is not the competency standard.

sources.title: O. Reg. 799/93: PROFESSIONAL MISCONDUCT
sources.evidence: Directing inadequately trained/incompetent performance of nursing functions is professional misconduct.

sources.title: 15.4 Nursing Standards of Delegation
sources.evidence: RN ensures required education and competencies before the person performs the care.
